title: Module 1 · Lesson 4 — Multi-agent topologies and when each one wins

lines: Picture a travel startup building an assistant that plans a two-week trip through Japan.
Flights, hotels, rail passes, and visas each need their own tools.
Version one is a single agent holding every tool.
Its context fills with hotel listings, and it forgets the traveller's budget.
Splitting into several agents helps, but only for three reasons.
First, specialisation: different prompts, tools, models, or permissions.
Second, context isolation: a researcher reads a mountain of sources and hands back a short brief.
Third, parallelism: independent questions run at once.
The price is handoff latency, duplicated tokens, and harder debugging.
And errors compound: four agents at ninety percent each are about sixty-six percent together.
The travel team picks the first of five topologies: a supervisor.
It owns the trip and routes flights, hotels, and visas to specialist workers.
Workers never talk to each other, so traces are clean and policy lives in one place.
The catch: the supervisor is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
In a swarm, agents hand control straight to each other, with no coordinator.
It's faster, but harder to trace, and two agents can bounce a task forever.
A pipeline runs agents in a fixed order: extract, analyse, draft, review.
Simple and traceable, but one failed stage stalls the chain.
A blackboard gives agents a shared workspace instead of messages.
Specialists build one evolving artefact together, like an incident timeline.
In a debate, agents argue across rounds, and a judge picks the winner.
It helps on hard judgement calls, at several times the cost.
How agents talk matters as much as the shape.
Hand over typed, structured artefacts, not raw transcripts.
Watch for handoff loops, lost context, and runaway cost.
Fix them with a global step budget and a structured handoff object.
On the exam, MCP connects agents to tools, and A2A connects agents to other agents.
For a researcher, coder, and reviewer team, pick the supervisor, then read on for the full comparison.
